title: Aerophagia and gastrointestinal symptoms during positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy in obstructive sleep apnea: a prospective questionnaire study
summary: Positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy is the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. During therapy, air can enter the esophagus and stomach (aerophagia). This may cause bloating, belching, a feeling of fullness or abdominal pain and can make therapy difficult. How often these symptoms occur, when they start and how they develop is hardly known. In this study, adults starting PAP therapy for the first time complete a short questionnaire about one week and about three months after the start of therapy. In addition, treatment data and usage data of the PAP device are analysed. Treatment is not changed. The aim is to detect symptoms and risk factors earlier and to make therapy better tolerated.

interventions.name: Adult patients with obstructive sleep apnea starting positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy for the first time at the Sleep Medicine Center of the Ruhrlandklinik Essen (CPAP, APAP, BiPAP or ASV; recruited as inpatients and via the outpatient sleep laboratory). criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age ≥ 18 years; sufficient German language skills to complete the questionnaires independently; indication for first-time PAP therapy (CPAP, APAP, BiPAP or ASV) for obstructive sleep apnea after current sleep medicine diagnostics (first-time use verified by the medical and nursing team); written informed consent to participate and to the use of telemonitoring data.
Exclusion criteria:
Pre-existing severe gastrointestinal symptoms with another likely main cause that would substantially bias attribution to PAP-related aerophagia; acute or severe gastrointestinal disease that markedly affects symptom perception or attribution (e.g. acute gastroenteritis, active inflammatory bowel disease); abdominal surgery of the gastrointestinal tract within three months before the respective questionnaire (exclusion for that time point only); inability to give informed consent.
